title: p99/p95 latency deep dive with Quantum Ware
summary: Deep dive on worst-case tail latency for Quantum Ware's chat inference workload. Discussed p95/p99 behavior, impact of batching and KV cache, streaming pros/cons, quantization tradeoffs, network hops (VPC peering vs private deployment), and mitigations. Agreed on next steps to run capture traces and a small benchmarking pilot on Redwood Dedicated and Private preview.
next_steps: Redwood to share kernel perf spreadsheet and suggested batching configs (Jordan) by 2027-03-19
Quantum Ware to share sample trace captures and payload distribution by 2027-03-20
Schedule 90-minute pilot planning session wk of 2027-03-22 (Maya to propose times)
action_items: Jordan Li (Redwood): prepare kernel/quantization perf sheet and example config snippets (due 2027-03-19)
Priya Rao (Quantum Ware): export 24h of request traces and sequence length histogram (due 2027-03-20)
Maya Alvarez (Redwood): send pricing template + Dedicated sizing options (due 2027-03-18)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro - I'm Maya, AE for Redwood, Jordan and Samir from the infra/solutions side are with me.
[00:12] Liam (Quantum Ware): Hi, Liam here, Priya and Diego on the line too, thanks. We reeeally want to understand our tail latency at p99, p95 for our streaming chat workload.
[00:26] Jordan (Redwood): Great, can you give a quick baseline - current infra and numbers?
[00:32] Priya (Quantum Ware): Yeah, we run a mix of 8k token prompts and lots of short completions, avg latency is 120 ms for short, p95 around 280 ms, p99 is spiky up to 1.6s, sometimes 3s during bursts, that's with our current managed provider.
[00:48] Diego (Quantum Ware): We do not have KV cache enabled in prod yet, just straight endpoints.
[00:55] Samir (Redwood): Ok so two big levers: KV/prefix cache and batching. Also streaming changes effective tail behavior. We want to separate model compute tail vs network hops and scheduling.
[01:10] Priya: How much does batching hurt p99? We've been told batching is great for throughput but it hurts tail - is that true?
[01:18] Jordan: Short answer: it depends. Small, adaptive batching with latency SLOs can actually reduce tail because it avoids head-of-line blocking when done right, but large fixed batches will increase per-request latency and amplify p99. The runtime uses continuous batching and we have per-route SLO-driven flush thresholds.
[01:35] Liam: What about streaming vs non-streaming? Our product streams tokens to users; does that change p95/p99 accounting?
[01:42] Samir: Yes - streaming breaks the tail into two concerns: time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token. p95 for time-to-first-token is usually dominated by network/hop setup and model decode start. p99 for end-to-end can be magnified by late tokens, KV cache misses, or long-running sequences.
[01:58] Priya: We're also doing VPC peering from our cloud into managed endpoints; we suspect network hops are adding 50-200ms. Any recommendations?
[02:07] Jordan: Network hops absolutely matter. We typically recommend colocating inference regionally, using VPC endpoints or Private deployment when you need sub-10ms inter-service latency. With VPC peering across regions you'll see variance - p99 worsens. For strict SLOs, Redwood Private in your VPC or on-prem reduces that unpredictability.
[02:26] Diego: What about KV cache warmup - you mentioned prefix caching earlier - how big an impact?
[02:31] Samir: Prefix/KV cache reduces compute substantially for repeated context; for retrieval use-cases it can drop per-token compute by up to 60% on warmed keys. The tail benefit is huge when cache hit rates are high because you avoid long model decode paths. But cold-miss storms (cache churn) can create bursts, so we recommend tiered cache warming and async prefetch for high-volume keys.
[02:53] Priya: Quantization - we're using int8 on some benches, aggressive quantization gives speed but has quality regressions. Any guidance?
[03:01] Jordan: We run quantization profiles per-model and per-workload. int8 on GPT-style models generally reduces latency 20-40% depending on kernel and sequence lengths; but for generation quality-sensitive flows you may see hallucination increases. Redwood Optimize suggests model/quant profiles and rollback plans; we can run a small A/B under your eval prompts.
[03:24] Liam: Can you talk about scheduling and kernel selection - sometimes we see single-request stalls while GPU switches kernels?
[03:31] Samir: Good point - kernel switches happen when sequence lengths vary or different attention mechanisms are used. Our runtime picks kernels dynamically and we have pre-compilation for common shapes. When there's a cold kernel path it adds overhead; you want to standardize sequence length buckets or pad to reduce variability. We also expose CPU/GPU affinity and reserved pools to avoid eviction pauses.
[03:54] Priya: Our probes show an extra 120ms on some p99s that we suspect are from network setup and TLS handshake to the endpoint. Any mitigations?
[04:02] Jordan: Keep connections warm with long-lived connections, use HTTP/2 or gRPC streaming, and prefer private network paths. For very low-latency use cases, a private deployment within your VPC avoids TLS-to-internet hops.
[04:15] Diego: What's Redwood Dedicated's typical p99 for 8k seqs if we use small batching and KV cache?
[04:21] Samir: On Dedicated with tuned batching, streaming on, and warm KV cache, p95 for short paths can be sub-200ms and p99 usually under 400-600ms for mixed workloads; long 8k generations will of course be higher but predictable. For strict sub-100ms SLOs you'd be looking at smaller models or more sharding and aggressive quant.
[04:42] Liam: We need numbers - can you run a pilot with our traces?
[04:46] Maya: Yes - Jordan can share the perf spreadsheet, and we can set up a short Dedicated pilot and a Private preview for you to run captured traces and compare p95/p99.
[04:56] Priya: On observability, what traces/logs will you need?
[05:00] Jordan: We need request_id, timestamps for client send, gateway receive, model start, token-first, token-last, sequence length, and headers showing connection route. The traces let us split network vs runtime vs kernel vs scheduling.
[05:12] Priya: We'll produce that, though some of our current logs are noisy.
[05:15] Liam: Any security/compliance concerns for Private? We need SOC2 type controls and KMS integration.
[05:20] Maya: Private includes customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and SOC2 controls; we'll share the security pack.
[05:27] Diego: Competitors - we've tried a couple providers, Bedrock had more stable p95 but higher cost, OpenAI was cheaper for short but p99 spikes.
[05:36] Samir: Sounds typical. Our approach is to make tail predictable with cache+batches+smart routing. Also can fallback to smaller variants during congestion.
[05:46] Maya: Quick recap of next steps: Jordan will share kernel/perf sheet and example batching configs, Priya will export traces, Maya will send pricing and Dedicated sizing. We'll schedule the pilot planning next week.
[05:58] Liam: Thanks all, that was useful.
[06:02] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and times.
